latin.2491: LIII. Jansenius autem eam Christi gratiam, quae hominem jam boni cognitione illustratum, & variis modis pulsatum, allectum, & sollicitatum ut bonum amplectatur, ad illud tandem reapse prosequendum efficaciter & certo determinat, non aliud esse vult, quam coelestem quandam atque ineffabilem suavitatem, seu spiritualem delectationem, qua voluntas praevenitur & flectitur ad volendum faciendumque quicquid Deus eam velle & facere constituerit. Nec enim ullum esse genus actionis aut voluntatis bonae, ullumve effectum gratiae efficacis, qui non isti Coelesti delectationi, tanquam verae gratiae Christi, veraeque causae tribuendum sit. Illam esse per quam bonum, quod praedicatur nobis, incipimus concupiscere: per quam bonum jam cogitatum pia voluntate credimus atque suscipimus. Sine coelitus infusa ejusmodi delectatione, nec orationem ullam Deo gratam fundi posse, nec Deum pure & caste diligi, nec cupiditatum nostrarum tentationibus resisti, nec denique ullum bonum opus fieri. Ut prolixe Doctor ille ex Augustino probare contendit. De gratia Christi salvatoris libro 4. cap. 1. & seqq.
latin.2492: LIV. Ut autem explicet quid sit ista coelestis suavitas & delectatio, quam veram Christi gratiam, ex sua & Augustini sententia esse existimat, distinguit in appetitu & in voluntate tres circa bonum actus. Primus est simplex amor, sive complacentia, quae est veluti quaedam coaptatio appetitus ad bonum ut sibi conveniens. Secundus est motus quidam inde consequens, qui dicitur desiderium, per quod appetitus tendit in bonum sibi conveniens & aptum. Tertius est quies in bono quod jam aliquis adeptus est. Et actus ille proprie dicitur gaudium & delectatio, per quam animus in bono praesenti, cum quadam satisfactione & fruitione conquiescit.
latin.2493: LV. Quanquam vero delectatio in tertio illo actu proprie consistat, nihilominus observat in prioribus actibus simplicis amoris & desiderii, inesse quandam delectationem: quia cum omnis amor ad delectationem, tanquam ad quietem ac centrum suum, per desiderium tendat, fieri non potest quin ipse motus quoque aliquid ex illa suavitate participet. Nam simul atque motus incipit, participat de quiete, quatenus etiam primum momentum motus habet partialem terminum suum.
latin.2494: LVI. Quod in amore ac desiderio rerum spiritualium, sapientiae, veritatis, sanctitatis, justitiae & charitatis, multo maxime locum habet. Nam qui diligit res terrenas, non hoc ipso quod eas diligit, etiam adipiscitur, nec tanquam in adeptis conquiescit, neque quasi fruens animo delectatur. Quisquis vero diligit justitiam, veritatem, sapientiam, charitatem, hoc ipso bona illa adipiscitur, habet, & possidet; & per hoc etiam iis cum delectatione fruitur, & cum fruitione delectatur. Adeoque qui diligit Deum, qui est ipsa aeterna sapientia, veritas, charitas, justitia, ipso quoque dilectionis actu, tanquam objectum suum possidente, fruitur & delectatur Deo. Unde sequitur etiam actibus amoris & desiderii, praesertim quum circa Deum & res divinas versantur, delectationis & suavitatis nomen recte tribui, ut fit passim ab Augustino.
latin.2495: LVII. Praeterea notandum est actus amoris & desiderii, quibus afficitur voluntas, vel deliberatos & liberos esse, qui praevia consultatione, ex certo rationis judicio eliciuntur: vel indeliberatos, & ita non liberos, qui nimirum ad objecti alicujus propositionem, in voluntate subito oriuntur, priusquam mens consultare & deliberare possit.
latin.2496: LVIII. Quibus animadversis, observat idem Doctor coelestem delectationem, in qua ponit Christi auxilium efficax, ad omnem piam operationem & bonum voluntatis actum, necessarium, non esse delectationem illam proprie dictam, per quam voluntas in bono praesenti acquiescit, & eo fruitur; & quae est desiderii, quo voluntas fertur in bonum, quasi terminus: nec etiam ullum esse voluntatis motum liberum atque deliberatum; Sed actum quendam indeliberatum coelitus immissum in voluntatem, & per quem, vel ei bonum propositum suaviter tantum placet, vel etiam in bonum appetendum commovetur. Qui actus coelitus immissus, licet voluntas eum libere non eliciat, ab ea tamen active procedit, & vitalis est illius quidam motus.
latin.2497: LIX. Istam autem delectationem in nullo amore, vel desiderio libero consistere, juxta Doctoris illius principia manifestum est. Quandoquidem etiam ad desiderandum & amandum Deum, & quodlibet verum ac spirituale bonum, libero voluntatis motu, necessaria est: cum desiderium & amor ejusmodi sint actus boni, qui sine suavitatis gratia non possunt a voluntate proficisci. Qua de re pluribus agit Jansenius, libro quarto de gratia Christi salvatoris capite undecimo, cujus titulus est, Delectatio ista coelestis, secundum Augustini mentem, est actus vitalis & indeliberatus animae: & quidem amoris ac desiderii praecedentis consensum, ac delectationem illam, quae & quies animi, & gaudium dicitur.
latin.2498: LX. Haec vero divinitus infusa delectatio, ex Authoris istius mente, ad bonum quemlibet actum voluntatis ideo necessaria est, quod secundum expressum Augustini pronunciatum, voluntas moveri nullo pacto potest, nisi aliquid occurrat quod delectet atque invitet animum. Nec enim quicquam amplectitur voluntas, quin prius erga illud aliquo delectationis sensu afficiatur. Quod locum habet, non tantum in bonis, sed etiam in malis. Nam voluntas non fertur in malum, nisi praeparetur atque impellatur praecedente quadam delectatione, qua malum sub falsa boni specie ipsi blanditur.
latin.2499: LXI. Cum vero saepe contingat hominis animum circa opposita aliquo delectationis sensu simul affici; ac praesertim in fidelibus, quamdiu corpus hoc mortale gerunt, lucta fit duarum delectationum, unius terrenae, alterius coelestis, unius noxiae, alterius beneficae: utralibet vicerit, animum secum pronum & consentientem trahit. Nec unquam aliter evenire potest, quam ut major delectatio voluntatem rapiat in illud quod magis delectat. Ac ubicunque animus, inter justitiam & peccatum constitutus, in diversa trahitur, quod amplius delectaverit, secundum illud operetur necesse est.
latin.2500: LXII. Quam suam sententiam Jansenius illustrat his Augustini verbis, ex commentario in epistolam ad Galatas desumptis, ubi Augustinus agens de fructibus spiritus, qui sunt gaudium, pax, longanimitas, benignitas, bonitas, fides, mansuetudo, continentia, Regnant, inquit, spirituales isti fructus in homine in quo peccata non regnant. Regnant autem ista bona, si tantum delectant, ut ipsa teneant animum in tentationibus, ne in peccati consensionem ruat. Quod enim amplius nos delectat, secundum id operemur necesse est. Ut verbi gratia, occurrit forma speciosae foeminae, & movet ad delectationem fornicationis: sed si plus delectat pulchritudo illa intima, & sincera species castitatis, per gratiam quae est in fide Christi, secundum hanc vivimus, & secundum hanc operamur; ut non regnante in nobis peccato, ad obediendum desideriis ejus, sed regnante justitia per charitatem, cum magna delectatione faciamus quicquid in ea Deo placere cognoscimus. Quod autem de castitate & fornicatione dixi, hoc de caeteris intelligi volui.
latin.2501: LXIII. Itaque illud efficax adjutorium divinae gratiae non in qualibet circa bonum delectatione ponit, sed in tali delectatione, quae in homine cui datur, omni delectatione opposita major sit, atque illam superet; & quam idcirco, cum Augustino, vocat Victricem delectationem. Si enim major sit carnis delectatio, nunquam illa quam spiritus infundit, a voluntate consensum impetrabit. Nam minor delectatio non potest majorem vincere: sed eam sequitur animus, quae magis eum afficiendo suavitate detinuerit. De gratia Christi salvat. lib. 4. cap. 6.
latin.2502: LXIV. Porro quanquam victrix illa delectatio, in qua Christi gratia medicinalis & efficax consistit, voluntatem ad bonum, secundum illius doctrinam, impellat infallibiliter, & bono, quod ita suave est, certo consentire faciat: nihilominus quae in uno victrix est, quia minor ei se opponit carnis delectatio, quaeque idcirco voluntatem in consensum inducit, in alio tamen majori & fortiori carnis delectatione vincetur, nec per eam flectetur voluntas, quam captivam abducet delectatio terrena potentior atque valentior.
latin.2503: LXV. Caeterum necessitatem victricis istius delectationis, quam oporteat coelitus infundi ad vincendas tentationes, & peragenda justitiae opera, ex voluntatis infirmitate petit, qua fit ut nihil boni amplecti possit, nisi delectet. Quia voluntas per se, & sua sola volendi libertate, interna voluptatis dolorisve impedimenta superare non potest. Nec homo ex se sufficit, ut Pelagiani volebant, ingenitis sibi motibus dare leges. Siquidem terrenae delectationes, ex innata homini concupiscentia ortae, voluntatem ita deprimunt, & a vero bono revocant, ut erigere se non possit, & in operationes coelo dignas prorumpere, nisi Deus immittat coelestem quandam delectationem atque suavitatem, terrenis illis majorem atque potentiorem, per quam carnalium concupiscentiarum visco expediatur, & in libertatem ex illa captivitate asseratur. Absque quo voluntas non potest bonum tam fortiter & intense velle, ut tentationem contrariam superet. Ut nec in ejus potestate situm est coelestibus pro libitu delectari, juxta illud Augustini ad Simplicianum, Quis habet in potestate tali viso attingi mentem suam, quo ejus voluntas moveatur ad fidem? Quis autem animo amplectitur aliquid quod eum non delectet? Aut quis habet in potestate, ut vel occurrat quod eum delectare possit, vel delectet quum occurrerit? Quum ergo nos ea delectant quibus proficiamus ad Deum, inspiratur hoc & praebetur gratia Dei, non nutu nostro & industria, aut operum meritis comparatur.
latin.2504: LXVI. Ex quibus & multis aliis similibus hanc conclusionem elicit Jansenius, Haec igitur volendi imbecillitas, quae ex terrenarum rerum delectationibus deorsum voluntatem ad creata atque carnalia diligenda deprimentibus, nascitur, vera causa est, cur delectatio justitiae, seu operis boni quod praecipitur, necessaria sit, qua sublevatus animus vel fortiter velle possit, quod jam tenuiter vult, vel etiam velle quod non vult. Cujus delectationis suavitate, nisi Deus voluntatem deliniverit, nunquam poterit ipsius praecepti justitiam vel implere, vel velle: sed si quos actus circa praeceptum exercere videatur, nonnisi in terrenarum concupiscentiarum ac delectationum, vel proprii fastus fructum terminabuntur. Coelestis enim illa suavitas mollit viam, ut voluntas ex carnalium rerum visco emergere possit, & seipsam in justitiam diligendam figere. Ex quo consequenter fit, ut si illa desit, voluntas veluti torpens ac mortua nihil omnino boni amplecti possit; quemadmodum etiam e contrario, nihil in carnalibus diligendo prosequi potest, nisi quod eam delectaverit. De gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 4. cap. 7.
latin.2505: LXVII. Caeterum hanc delectationis coelestis necessitatem ad volendum atque operandum, & voluntatis nostrae infirmitatem, qua fit, ut nec moveri ad bonum possit, nisi quid delectaverit, nec inter duo quae delectant aliud eligere, quam quod delectando superaverit, sedulo monet author ille, non ex essentia & natura voluntatis, sed ex ejus poena proficisci. Nec enim putat hanc esse naturam humanae voluntatis absolute consideratae, ut non possit libere bonum objectum prosequi, nisi prius delectaverit: ac multo minus existimat necessarium esse, ut viso objecto bono, voluntas tangatur aliqua delectatione.
latin.2506: LXVIII. Itaque totum istud tribuit imbecillitati cuidam voluntatis per peccatum contractae, & quae inter peccati poenas numeranda est. Nec enim ante peccatum, juxta illius hypotheses, delectatio ulla voluntati dominabatur, & in alterutram partem illam flectebat ac determinabat, efficaciter ejus consensum eliciendo. Nam priusquam homo per peccatum integritate sua primaeva cecidisset, nulla terrenarum rerum delectatio voluntatem ejus ad malum sollicitabat & illiciebat; idque quoniam omnis ejusmodi delectatio nascitur ex concupiscentia, quae peccati fructus est. Ac proinde primum peccatum primi hominis sine delectatione praecedente perpetratum est. Delectatio quippe prima secuta est perversam voluntatem, non voluntas delectationem. Siquidem omnis repugnantia bonae voluntatis supplicium est malae; quod Deus creaturae rationali non infligit immeritae.
latin.2507: LXIX. Quod spectat autem bonas actiones, ea quidem gratia primus homo praeditus erat, ut illas exercere posset, iisque debite & perfecte fungi: sed gratia illa non erat ejusmodi, ut eum faceret velle & operari: quoniam ejus libero arbitrio subjacebat, & penes eum erat gratia ista uti, vel non uti. Ac proinde in eo locum non habebat illa delectatio victrix, quae liberum sibi subjicit arbitrium, & voluntatem ad bonum movet efficaciter & infallibiliter. Unde manifesto sequitur, illam quae jam obtinet delectationis victricis necessitatem ad bene operandum, ex ipsa voluntatis natura non oriri. Nam alioquin oporteret illam in homine perpetuam fuisse: cum tamen in homine integro locum non habuerit, nec etiam fuerit ei necessaria.
latin.2508: LXX. Itaque quod coelestem illam delectationem ad actus bonos necessariam reddit, non aliud est, juxta hunc doctorem, quam voluntatis humanae corruptio & depravatio. Quia, scilicet, voluntas per peccatum primi hominis in libidinum imperium praecipitata est. Ex quo fit ut in omnibus actionibus ante gratiam, delectatione quadam libidinosa praeeunte ac titillante provocetur, cui consentiendo peccat, & si sibi relinquatur, non consentire non potest. Cui malo curando immittitur a Deo delectatio boni seu justitiae, tanquam unica aegrotae voluntatis medicina, qua ut directe contraria morbo quo affligitur, extorquetur ejus in bonum, quod ab ea Deus postulat, consensus; & ita voluntas retorquetur sursum, ut blandienti delectantique spiritui affixa, & quasi suspensa ex Deo, non amplius in veterem libidinis servitutem detrahatur. Quae pluribus diducit Jansenius cap. 9. libri saepius jam citati.
latin.2509: LXXI. Ex quibus omnibus facile colligitur quomodo conveniat sententia Jansenii cum sententia Thomistarum, & quomodo ab illa discrepet, circa gratiam quam sufficientem, & circa eam quam efficacem vocant. Nempe, quod spectat gratiam quae sufficiens dicitur, Jansenius cum illis agnoscit eos ipsos qui non convertuntur, nec bene operantur, multiplicem a Deo gratiam accipere; & non solum eorum intellectum illuminari, sed & voluntatem variis gratiae motibus percelli: Nec diffitetur, acceptis ejusmodi gratiae auxiliis, hominem vere dici, posse converti, & bene operari. Et vice versa Thomistae fatentur omnibus illis qui non convertuntur, nec bene operantur, deesse auxilium quoddam plane necessarium ut quis actu convertatur & bene operetur.
latin.2510: LXXII. In eo vero discrimen est quod Thomistae gratiam, quam actu non sequitur bona operatio, nihilominus dicunt sufficientem esse, & per illam dari potentiam bene operandi proximam & completam. Quod negat Jansenius & qui eum sequuntur. Qua in re apparet meram esse logomachiam & quaestionem de nomine. Quandoquidem Jansenius non propter aliud negat gratiam ejusmodi sufficientem esse, & per eam dari potentiam proximam bene operandi, quam quia deest illi auxilium aliquod ad bonam actionem plane necessarium, quod Thomistae concedunt.

sections.title: Jansenius: efficacious grace is a heavenly delight
sections.pass_a: LIII. But Jansenius wills that that grace of Christ, which man already illuminated by knowledge of good, and in various ways knocked at, allured, and solicited that he embrace the good, at length efficaciously and certainly determines to actually pursuing it, is nothing else than a certain heavenly and ineffable sweetness, or spiritual delight, by which the will is prevented and bent to willing and doing whatever God has determined that it will and do. For there is no kind of action or of good will, nor any effect of efficacious grace, which is not to be attributed to this Heavenly delight, as to the true grace of Christ, and true cause. That it is that through which we begin to desire the good which is preached to us: through which we believe and take up with pious will the good already thought. Without such delight infused from heaven, neither can any prayer pleasing to God be poured out, nor God be loved purely and chastely, nor the temptations of our desires be resisted, nor finally any good work be done. As that Doctor at length strives to prove from Augustine. On the grace of Christ the saviour book 4. chap. 1. and following.
pass_b: Thesis LIII. Jansenius holds that the grace of Christ which, once a person has been enlightened with knowledge of the good and in various ways prompted, drawn and urged to embrace it, finally determines him effectively and surely to pursue it in fact, is nothing other than a heavenly and inexpressible sweetness, or spiritual delight. By it the will is anticipated and bent to will and do whatever God has resolved that it should will and do.

For there is no kind of good action or good will, and no effect of efficacious grace, that is not to be ascribed to this heavenly delight as to the true grace of Christ and its true cause. It is by this delight that we begin to desire the good preached to us, and by it that, with devout will, we believe and take up the good we have already thought of.

Without such a delight poured in from heaven, no prayer pleasing to God can be offered, God cannot be loved purely and chastely, the temptations of our desires cannot be resisted, and in short no good work can be done. So that doctor labours at length to prove from Augustine: De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapters 1 and following.

sections.title: Three acts of the appetite: love, desire, delight
sections.pass_a: LIV. But that he may explain what that heavenly sweetness and delight is, which he judges, from his own and Augustine's opinion, to be the true grace of Christ, he distinguishes in the appetite and in the will three acts about the good. The first is simple love, or complacency, which is as it were a certain fitting of the appetite to the good as fitting to itself. The second is a certain motion thence following, which is called desire, through which the appetite tends to the good fitting and apt to itself. The third is rest in the good which someone has already obtained. And that act is properly called joy and delight, through which the mind rests in a present good, with a certain satisfaction and fruition.
pass_b: Thesis LIV. To explain what this heavenly sweetness and delight is, which in his own view and Augustine's is the true grace of Christ, he distinguishes three acts of the appetite and of the will with respect to the good. The first is simple love, or complacency: a kind of adjusting of the appetite to the good as suited to it.

The second is a movement that follows from this, called desire, by which the appetite reaches out toward the good that suits and fits it. The third is rest in a good one has already gained; and this act is properly called joy and delight, by which the mind settles in a present good with a certain satisfaction and enjoyment.

sections.title: Even love and desire share in delight
sections.pass_a: LV. But although delight properly consists in that third act, nevertheless he observes that in the prior acts of simple love and desire, there is a certain delight: because since every love tends through desire to delight, as to its rest and centre, it cannot be that the very motion also does not partake something of that sweetness. For as soon as motion begins, it partakes of rest, inasmuch as even the first moment of motion has its partial term.
pass_b: Thesis LV. Although delight properly consists in that third act, he observes that a certain delight is present even in the earlier acts of simple love and desire. Since every love tends by way of desire toward delight, as to its rest and centre, the movement itself cannot fail to share something of that sweetness. As soon as a movement begins it has a share in rest, inasmuch as even the first moment of a movement has its own partial end.

sections.title: Love of spiritual goods already possesses and enjoys them
sections.pass_a: LVI. Which holds place by far most of all in the love and desire of spiritual things, of wisdom, truth, holiness, justice and charity. For he who loves earthly things, does not by this very thing that he loves them, also obtain them, nor rest as in things obtained, nor is delighted as enjoying in mind. But whoever loves justice, truth, wisdom, charity, by this very thing obtains, has, and possesses those goods; and through this also enjoys them with delight, and is delighted with enjoyment. And so he who loves God, who is the eternal wisdom itself, truth, charity, justice, by the very act also of love, as possessing its object, enjoys and is delighted in God. Whence it follows that to the acts also of love and desire, especially when they are occupied about God and divine things, the name of delight and sweetness is rightly attributed, as is done everywhere by Augustine.
pass_b: Thesis LVI. This holds good most of all, by far, in the love and desire of spiritual things: wisdom, truth, holiness, righteousness and charity. Whoever loves earthly things does not gain them simply by loving them, nor rest in them as things gained, nor take delight in enjoying them in his mind.

But whoever loves righteousness, truth, wisdom or charity by that very fact gains, has and possesses those goods, and so enjoys them with delight and delights in enjoying them. So whoever loves God, who is eternal wisdom itself, truth, charity and righteousness, enjoys God and delights in him by the very act of love, which possesses its object.
It follows that the names of delight and sweetness are rightly given to acts of love and desire as well, especially when they concern God and divine things, as Augustine does throughout.

sections.title: Deliberate and indeliberate acts of love and desire
sections.pass_a: LVII. Further it is to be noted that the acts of love and desire, by which the will is affected, are either deliberate and free, which are elicited with prior consultation, from a certain judgment of reason: or indeliberate, and so not free, which namely at the proposal of some object, arise suddenly in the will, before the mind can consult and deliberate.
pass_b: Thesis LVII. Note also that the acts of love and desire that affect the will are of two kinds. Some are deliberate and free, drawn out after weighing the matter, from a definite judgment of reason. Others are indeliberate and therefore not free: they spring up in the will all at once when some object is put before it, before the mind is able to weigh and deliberate.

choices.why: An act arising before the mind deliberates (LVII), as opposed to a free, deliberate act.

sections.title: The heavenly delight is an indeliberate act sent from heaven
sections.pass_a: LVIII. Which things being noticed, the same Doctor observes that the heavenly delight, in which he places the efficacious help of Christ, necessary to every pious operation and good act of the will, is not that delight properly so called, through which the will rests in a present good, and enjoys it; and which is of desire, by which the will is borne to good, as a term: nor yet is it any free and deliberate motion of the will; But a certain indeliberate act sent from heaven into the will, and through which, either the good proposed only sweetly pleases it, or it is even moved to desiring the good. Which act sent from heaven, although the will does not elicit it freely, yet proceeds actively from it, and is a certain vital motion of it.
pass_b: Thesis LVIII. With these points in view, the same doctor observes that the heavenly delight in which he places Christ's efficacious aid, needed for every devout action and good act of the will, is not delight in the proper sense, by which the will rests in a present good and enjoys it and which is the end point of the desire by which the will is carried toward the good. Nor is it any free and deliberate movement of the will.

It is an indeliberate act sent into the will from heaven, through which the good put before the will either simply pleases it sweetly or even stirs it to desire that good. Although the will does not elicit this heaven-sent act freely, the act still proceeds from the will actively and is a vital movement of the will.

sections.title: Not a free love or desire (book 4, chapter 11)
sections.pass_a: LIX. But that this delight consists in no free love, or desire, is manifest according to that Doctor's principles. Since it is necessary even for desiring and loving God, and any true and spiritual good, with a free motion of the will: since desire and love of this kind are good acts, which without the grace of sweetness cannot proceed from the will. Of which matter Jansenius treats at more length, in the fourth book on the grace of Christ the saviour chapter eleven, whose title is, This heavenly delight, according to Augustine's mind, is a vital and indeliberate act of the soul: and indeed of love and desire preceding consent, and that delight, which is called both rest of the mind, and joy.
pass_b: Thesis LIX. On that doctor's principles it is plain that this delight does not consist in any free love or desire. It is needed even in order to desire and love God, or any true spiritual good, by a free movement of the will, since such desire and love are good acts, which cannot come from the will without the grace of sweetness.

Jansenius deals with this more fully in De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapter 11, whose heading is: 'This heavenly delight, in Augustine's mind, is a vital and indeliberate act of the soul; that is, an act of the love and desire that come before consent and before the delight that is also called the mind's rest and joy.'

sections.title: Why delight is needed: the will moves only toward what delights
sections.pass_a: LX. But this delight divinely infused, from that Author's mind, is therefore necessary to any good act of the will, because according to the express pronouncement of Augustine, the will can in no way be moved, unless something occurs which delights and invites the mind. For the will embraces nothing, without being first affected toward it by some sense of delight. Which holds place, not only in good things, but also in evil. For the will is not borne to evil, unless it be prepared and impelled by some preceding delight, by which evil under a false appearance of good flatters it.
pass_b: Thesis LX. In that author's view this divinely infused delight is needed for every good act of the will because, by Augustine's express statement, the will cannot be moved in any way unless something comes before it that delights and invites the mind. The will embraces nothing unless it is first touched toward it by some sense of delight.

This holds not only for good things but for evil ones too. The will is not carried toward evil unless some prior delight prepares and drives it, through which evil coaxes it under a false show of good.

lemmas.gloss: the will can in no way be moved

lemmas.latin: nisi aliquid occurrat quod delectet atque invitet animum

sections.title: Two delights in conflict: the stronger carries the will
sections.pass_a: LXI. But since it often happens that a man's mind is affected at the same time by some sense of delight about opposite things; and especially in the faithful, as long as they bear this mortal body, there is a struggle of two delights, one earthly, the other heavenly, one harmful, the other beneficial: whichever has conquered, draws the mind with itself prone and consenting. Nor can it ever turn out otherwise, than that the greater delight snatches the will into that which delights more. And wherever the mind, placed between justice and sin, is drawn in different directions, it is necessary that it work according to that which has delighted more.
pass_b: Thesis LXI. A person's mind is often touched at once by some sense of delight toward opposite things. Especially in believers, as long as they carry this mortal body, there is a struggle between two delights, one earthly and the other heavenly, one harmful and the other helpful; and whichever wins draws the mind after it, inclined and consenting.

It can never turn out otherwise than that the greater delight carries the will off toward what delights it more. Wherever the mind stands between righteousness and sin and is pulled two ways, it must act according to whatever has delighted it more.

whichever has conquered

lemmas.gloss: it is necessary that it work according to that which has delighted more

sections.title: Augustine on Galatians: whatever delights us more, we must act on
sections.pass_a: LXII. Which opinion of his Jansenius illustrates with these words of Augustine, taken from the commentary on the epistle to the Galatians, where Augustine treating of the fruits of the spirit, which are joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faith, meekness, continence, These spiritual fruits, he says, reign in the man in whom sins do not reign. But these goods reign, if they delight so much, that they themselves hold the mind in temptations, lest it rush into consent of sin. For what delights us more, according to that it is necessary we work. As for example, the form of a beautiful woman meets one, and moves to the delight of fornication: but if that inward beauty delights more, and the sincere appearance of chastity, through the grace which is in the faith of Christ, according to this we live, and according to this we work; that sin not reigning in us, to obey its desires, but justice reigning through charity, with great delight we do whatever we know in it to please God. But what I have said of chastity and fornication, I wished to be understood of the rest.
pass_b: Thesis LXII. Jansenius illustrates his view with these words of Augustine from the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, where, treating the fruits of the Spirit (joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control), he says: 'These spiritual fruits reign in the person in whom sins do not reign. These goods reign if they delight so much that they hold the mind firm in temptations, so that it does not fall into consenting to sin. For whatever delights us more, we must act according to it.

'For example, the form of a beautiful woman comes before us and stirs us to the delight of fornication; but if that inner beauty and the pure face of chastity delight us more, through the grace that is in faith in Christ, then we live by it and act by it. So, with sin not reigning in us to make us obey its desires, but righteousness reigning through charity, we do with great delight whatever we know pleases God in it. What I have said of chastity and fornication I mean to be understood of the rest.'

sections.title: The efficacious help is the delight that is greater: victorious delight
sections.pass_a: LXIII. Therefore he places that efficacious help of divine grace not in any delight whatever about the good, but in such a delight, as in the man to whom it is given, is greater than every opposite delight, and overcomes it; and which therefore, with Augustine, he calls Victorious delight. For if the delight of the flesh be greater, never will that which the spirit infuses obtain consent from the will. For the lesser delight cannot conquer the greater: but the mind follows that which by affecting it more has held it with sweetness. On the grace of Christ the saviour book 4. chap. 6.
pass_b: Thesis LXIII. So he places that efficacious aid of divine grace not in just any delight in the good, but in a delight that, in the person to whom it is given, is greater than every opposing delight and overcomes it; and for this reason he calls it, with Augustine, 'victorious delight'.

If the delight of the flesh is greater, the delight that the spirit pours in will never win the will's consent. A lesser delight cannot overcome a greater; the mind follows whichever delight has held it more strongly by the sweetness with which it touches it. De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapter 6.

sections.title: Victorious in one person, overcome in another
sections.pass_a: LXIV. Further although that victorious delight, in which the medicinal and efficacious grace of Christ consists, according to his doctrine, impels the will to good infallibly, and makes it certainly consent to the good, which is thus sweet: nevertheless that which in one is victorious, because a lesser delight of the flesh opposes itself to it, and which therefore brings the will into consent, in another yet will be conquered by a greater and stronger delight of the flesh, nor will the will be bent through it, which a more powerful and stronger earthly delight will lead away captive.
pass_b: Thesis LXIV. Although, on his teaching, that victorious delight in which Christ's healing and efficacious grace consists drives the will to the good infallibly and makes it surely consent to the good that is so sweet, nevertheless a delight that wins in one person, because the delight of the flesh opposing it there is weaker, and so brings the will to consent, will in another person be overcome by a greater and stronger delight of the flesh. There it will not bend the will, which a mightier and stronger earthly delight will lead away captive.

lemmas.gloss: impels infallibly

sections.title: Why the victorious delight is needed: the will's weakness; Augustine to Simplicianus
sections.pass_a: LXV. However the necessity of that victorious delight, which must be infused from heaven to overcome temptations, and to perform the works of justice, he seeks from the infirmity of the will, by which it comes about that it can embrace nothing good, unless it delights. Because the will by itself, and by its sole liberty of willing, cannot overcome the inner hindrances of pleasure or pain. Nor is man sufficient of himself, as the Pelagians would have it, to give laws to the motions inborn in him. Since earthly delights, sprung from the concupiscence innate in man, so press down the will, and call it back from the true good, that it cannot raise itself, and break forth into operations worthy of heaven, unless God sends in a certain heavenly delight and sweetness, greater and more powerful than those earthly ones, through which it may be freed from the birdlime of carnal desires, and be set into liberty out of that captivity. Without which the will cannot will the good so strongly and intensely, that it overcomes the contrary temptation. As neither is it placed in its power to be delighted by heavenly things at pleasure, according to that of Augustine to Simplicianus, Who has it in his power that his mind be touched by such a sight, by which his will may be moved to faith? But who embraces in mind anything which does not delight him? Or who has it in his power, either that there occur what can delight him, or that it delight when it has occurred? When therefore those things delight us by which we may advance to God, this is inspired and furnished by the grace of God, not obtained by our nod and industry, or by the merits of works.
pass_b: Thesis LXV. He traces the need for that victorious delight, which must be poured in from heaven to overcome temptations and to carry out the works of righteousness, to the weakness of the will, which makes it unable to embrace anything good unless it delights. The will by itself, with only its freedom of willing, cannot overcome the inner obstacles of pleasure or pain; nor is a person able of himself, as the Pelagians claimed, to lay down laws for the impulses born in him.

Earthly delights arising from the concupiscence innate in human beings so weigh down the will and call it back from the true good that it cannot lift itself up and break out into actions worthy of heaven, unless God sends a heavenly delight and sweetness, greater and stronger than those earthly ones. By it the will is freed from the birdlime of carnal desires and set at liberty from that captivity. Without it the will cannot will the good so strongly and intensely as to overcome the opposing temptation.

Nor is it in the will's power to take delight in heavenly things at its pleasure, as Augustine says to Simplicianus: 'Who has it in his power that his mind should be touched by a sight that would move his will to faith? Who embraces in his mind anything that does not delight him? Or who has it in his power either that something able to delight him should come before him, or that it should delight him when it comes? So when the things by which we advance toward God delight us, this is inspired and given by God's grace; it is not obtained at our own bidding and by our own effort, or by the merit of our works.'

sections.title: Jansenius's conclusion (book 4, chapter 7)
sections.pass_a: LXVI. From which and many other similar things Jansenius draws this conclusion, This weakness therefore of willing, which arises from the delights of earthly things pressing down the will to loving created and carnal things, is the true cause, why the delight of justice, or of the good work which is commanded, is necessary, by which the mind raised up may either strongly will, what it already weakly wills, or even will what it does not will. Unless God has soothed the will by the sweetness of which delight, it will never be able either to fulfil, or to will the justice of the precept itself: but if it seem to exercise any acts about the precept, they will be terminated only in the fruit of earthly desires and delights, or of its own pride. For that heavenly sweetness softens the way, that the will may be able to emerge from the birdlime of carnal things, and fix itself in loving justice. From which it consequently comes about, that if it be lacking, the will as it were torpid and dead can embrace nothing at all of good; as also on the contrary, it can pursue nothing in loving carnal things, except what has delighted it. On the grace of Christ the saviour book 4. chap. 7.
pass_b: Thesis LXVI. From these and many similar passages Jansenius draws this conclusion: 'This weakness of willing, which arises from the delights of earthly things that press the will down to love created and carnal things, is the true reason why the delight of righteousness, that is, of the good work commanded, is necessary. Lifted up by it, the mind can either will strongly what it already wills feebly, or even will what it does not will.

'Unless God has softened the will with the sweetness of this delight, it will never be able either to fulfil or to will the righteousness of the commandment itself; and if it seems to perform some acts concerning the commandment, they will end only in the fruit of earthly desires and delights, or of its own pride. That heavenly sweetness smooths the way so that the will can get free of the birdlime of carnal things and fix itself on loving righteousness.

'It follows that if this delight is lacking, the will, as if numb and dead, can embrace nothing good at all; just as, conversely, in loving carnal things it can pursue nothing except what has delighted it.' De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 4, chapter 7.

lemmas.gloss: This weakness therefore of willing

lemmas.latin: vel fortiter velle possit, quod jam tenuiter vult
lemmas.gloss: may either strongly will, what it already weakly wills

sections.title: This need comes from the will's punishment, not its nature
sections.pass_a: LXVII. However this necessity of heavenly delight for willing and working, and the infirmity of our will, by which it comes about, that neither can it be moved to good, unless something has delighted, nor choose between two things which delight another than that which has prevailed by delighting, that author carefully warns proceeds not from the essence and nature of the will, but from its punishment. For he does not think this to be the nature of the human will considered absolutely, that it cannot freely pursue a good object, unless it has first delighted: and much less does he judge it necessary, that when a good object is seen, the will be touched with some delight.
pass_b: Thesis LXVII. That author is careful to point out that this need of heavenly delight for willing and acting, and the weakness of our will that makes it unable to be moved to the good unless something has delighted it, or to choose between two delightful things anything other than the one that has prevailed by delighting, comes not from the essence and nature of the will but from its punishment.

He does not think that the nature of the human will, considered in itself, is such that it cannot freely pursue a good object unless that object has first delighted it. Still less does he think it necessary that, when a good object is seen, the will be touched with some delight.

lemmas.latin: non ex essentia & natura voluntatis, sed ex ejus poena proficisci

sections.title: Before the fall no delight ruled the will; the first sin had no delight before it
sections.pass_a: LXVIII. Therefore he attributes all that to a certain weakness of the will contracted through sin, and which is to be numbered among the penalties of sin. For before sin, according to his hypotheses, no delight ruled the will, and bent and determined it to either side, by efficaciously eliciting its consent. For before man through sin fell from his primeval integrity, no delight of earthly things solicited and enticed his will to evil; and that because every delight of this kind is born from concupiscence, which is the fruit of sin. And therefore the first sin of the first man was committed without preceding delight. For delight first followed the perverse will, not the will delight. Since every resistance of the good will is the punishment of the evil one; which God does not inflict on a rational creature undeserving.
pass_b: Thesis LXVIII. So he ascribes all this to a weakness of the will contracted through sin, which is to be counted among the punishments of sin. On his assumptions, before sin no delight ruled the will, bending and determining it to one side or the other by effectively drawing out its consent.

Before man fell from his original integrity through sin, no delight in earthly things urged and enticed his will toward evil, since every such delight is born of concupiscence, which is the fruit of sin. The first sin of the first man was therefore committed with no delight going before it: the first delight followed the perverse will, not the will the delight. For every resistance to a good will is the punishment of an evil will, and God does not inflict it on a rational creature that has not deserved it.

sections.title: Adam's grace was not victorious delight
sections.pass_a: LXIX. But as regards good actions, the first man was indeed endowed with grace, that he could exercise them, and perform them duly and perfectly: but that grace was not such, that it made him will and work: since it lay subject to his free choice, and it was in his power to use that grace, or not to use it. And therefore in him that victorious delight had no place, which subjects free choice to itself, and moves the will to good efficaciously and infallibly. Whence it manifestly follows, that that necessity of victorious delight for working well which now obtains, does not arise from the very nature of the will. For otherwise it would have been necessary that it be perpetual in man: whereas yet in man unfallen it had no place, nor was it even necessary to him.
pass_b: Thesis LXIX. As for good actions, the first man was indeed endowed with grace so that he could perform them and carry them out duly and perfectly. But that grace was not such as to make him will and act, since it was subject to his free choice and it lay with him to use it or not to use it. So the victorious delight that brings free choice under itself and moves the will to the good effectively and infallibly had no place in him.

It plainly follows that the present need of victorious delight for acting well does not arise from the nature of the will itself. Otherwise it would have had to be permanent in man, whereas in man unfallen it had no place and was not even necessary to him.

sections.title: The cause is the will's corruption; delight as its one medicine (chapter 9)
sections.pass_a: LXX. Therefore what renders that heavenly delight necessary for good acts, is nothing else, according to this doctor, than the corruption and depravity of the human will. Because, namely, the will through the sin of the first man has been cast headlong into the dominion of lusts. From which it comes about that in all actions before grace, it is provoked by a certain lustful delight going before and tickling, by consenting to which it sins, and if it be left to itself, it cannot not consent. For curing which evil there is sent by God the delight of good or of justice, as the only medicine of the sick will, by which, as directly contrary to the disease with which it is afflicted, its consent to the good which God demands of it is wrung out; and so the will is twisted back upward, that fixed to the spirit soothing and delighting, and as it were hung from God, it may no longer be dragged down into the old slavery of lust. Which things Jansenius draws out at more length in chap. 9. of the book already often cited.
pass_b: Thesis LXX. On this doctor's view, then, what makes that heavenly delight necessary for good acts is nothing other than the corruption and depravity of the human will, which through the first man's sin has been thrown headlong under the rule of lusts. So in every action before grace it is roused by some lustful delight that goes before it and tickles it; by consenting to that delight it sins, and if left to itself it cannot fail to consent.

To cure this evil God sends the delight of the good, that is, of righteousness, as the sick will's one medicine. Because it runs directly against the disease afflicting the will, it wrings from the will the consent to the good that God requires of it. So the will is turned back upward, so that, fastened to the spirit that soothes and delights it and, as it were, hanging from God, it is no longer dragged down into its old slavery to lust. Jansenius develops this at length in chapter 9 of the book already cited several times.

sections.title: Where Jansenius and the Thomists agree on sufficient grace
sections.pass_a: LXXI. From all which it is easily gathered how the opinion of Jansenius agrees with the opinion of the Thomists, and how it differs from it, concerning the grace which they call sufficient, and concerning that which they call efficacious. Namely, as regards the grace which is called sufficient, Jansenius acknowledges with them that those very ones who are not converted, nor work well, receive manifold grace from God; and that not only is their intellect illuminated, but also the will is struck by various motions of grace: Nor does he deny, such helps of grace being received, that a man is truly said, to be able to be converted, and to work well. And conversely the Thomists confess that to all those who are not converted, nor work well, there is lacking a certain help plainly necessary that one may actually be converted and work well.
pass_b: Thesis LXXI. From all this it is easy to see how Jansenius's view agrees with the Thomists' and how it differs from theirs on the grace they call sufficient and the grace they call efficacious. As for the grace called sufficient, Jansenius grants with them that even those who are not converted and do not act well receive manifold grace from God, and that not only is their intellect enlightened but their will too is struck by various motions of grace.

Nor does he deny that, once such aids of grace are received, a person is truly said to be able to be converted and to act well. Conversely, the Thomists admit that all those who are not converted and do not act well lack an aid that is plainly necessary for anyone actually to be converted and act well.

sections.title: The difference: a battle of words about the name 'sufficient'
sections.pass_a: LXXII. But in this is the difference that the Thomists say that grace, which good operation does not actually follow, is nevertheless sufficient, and that through it is given a proximate and complete power of working well. Which Jansenius and those who follow him deny. In which matter it appears to be a mere logomachy and a question about a name. Since Jansenius denies grace of this kind to be sufficient, and that through it is given the proximate power of working well, for no other reason than because there is lacking to it some help plainly necessary for good action, which the Thomists concede.
pass_b: Thesis LXXII. The difference is this: the Thomists say that grace which good action does not in fact follow is nevertheless sufficient, and that through it a proximate and complete power of acting well is given. Jansenius and his followers deny this.

Here the dispute is plainly a mere battle of words, a question about a name. For Jansenius denies that such grace is sufficient, and that it gives the proximate power of acting well, for one reason only: it lacks an aid that is plainly necessary for good action, as the Thomists themselves concede.
